Hi Romain,

thanks for your considerations.

On Jul 2, 2009, at 5:03 , Romain Francois wrote:

> Hello,
>
> Here is below a method "objectNames" for the REXPEnvironment class to
> grab the names of the symbols that are in the environment.
>
>     /**
>      * @return the names of the objects in this environment
>      */
>     public String[] objectNames( boolean all) throws  
> REngineException {
>         String cmd = "ls(" ;
>         if( all ){
>             cmd  = cmd + "all.names = TRUE" ;
>         }
>         cmd = cmd + ")";
>         String[] names = eng.parseAndEval( "ls()", this, true
> ).asStrings() ;
>         return names;
>     }
>

What you're doing there is more like  
getNamesOfObjectsInGlobalEnvironment() and that's very specialized  
(and trivially just "ls()"), so not necessarily worth a wrapper.  
Admittedly environment support is currently incomplete (mostly because  
it is not supported by Rserve), but in JRI the canonical way is to use  
rniListEnv() which works on any environment object. This just needs to  
be exposed at the REngine [and later possibly at REXPEnvironment] level.


> A collateral issue is that the JRIEngine pretends it does not know  
> about
> the REXPEnvironment class:
>
> /** special, global references */
>     public REXPReference globalEnv, emptyEnv, baseEnv, nullValueRef;
>
> where the three first should be REXPEnvironment I think.
>

Nope for several reasons. First, those are all references to special R  
objects - and that's the whole point of those constants, so you can  
use them when passing objects to R. Second, there is no native  
representation of environments in Java (and they have pass-by- 
reference semantics), so you can only represent them as a reference.  
The REXPEnvironment is kind of placeholder for now - it should  
probably just wrap around a reference at some point and route the  
accessor methods accordingly (not high on the ToDo list, because it's  
not supported by Rserve anyway).


> and (probably a more serious problem):
>
> BeanShell> r.getClass()
> class org.rosuda.REngine.JRI.JRIEngine
> BeanShell> env = r.parseAndEval( "globalenv()" )
> BeanShell> env == null
>

See above.

Cheers,
Simon

messages.body_plain:
Martin,

Thanks for your response concerning this.  I hadn't realized that there
was so much variation in the mapping of the key modifiers across
platforms.  As I indicated, I originally assumed the difference was in
the Java implementation and I wound up installing three or four
different Java versions over the last few months trying to solve the 
problem.  I now see that the solution of using Shift-Win-Alt for 
modifying selections works in all recent Java versions that I have tried 
on this computer (running the Gnome interface under Fedora 10 Linux).

Over the last couple of weeks I have been very busy using Mondrian while
finishing up a manuscript for publication and I haven't had much time to
explore the keymapping on my Fedora Linux computer.  I have found that
by default, the computer runs xmodmap at startup and makes some
assignments to the Shift, Alt, and Win keys.  I can see how that is
done, but I don't know what codes should be assigned to make the
Shift-Alt combination work as desired in Mondrian.

If someone knows what keycodes to assign, I would be happy to know.
However, I am not asking you or anyone else to spend any time on my
behalf in sorting out this issue right now.  It is quite easy for me to
use the Shift-Win-Alt combination for modifying selections and I have
become used to it now.  If I get some time later this summer, I will 
look further into the issue and let you know what I find.

By the way, I now see a serious typo in my original message that may
have confused some readers.  As you figured out, in my first sentence I 
meant to say that "I have been frustrated that when using selections I 
could _not_ augment my current selection using the SHIFT-ALT key 
combination."

Thanks very much for the great software.  I use it all the time now when 
exploring new datasets.

Bill

interpretation of values by REXPLogical makes is more dangerous. One

instead of the raw values asa this may change.

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

For a while now I wanted to have an interface beteen R and Google
Docs.  Duncan Temple Lang has a package RGoogleDocs on OmegaHat
that uses rcurl, XML and basic POST and GET commands.  The
package is currently not working and I would prefer not to work
at that level, but to use the higher level Java API classes that
Google makes available.

One good reason for this is that occasionally Google changes the
XML protocol basics and then you have a lot of things to change in
your code.  However the Java API is stable, and should be easier
to maintain in the long run.  Also, Java seems to be the prefered
development language for the Google developers.  All the new
features appear in the Java API first, and then later show up in
other languages C#, Python, PHP, etc.  I think that the original
RGoogleDocs package suffered from an upgrade problem.

Following the Google
tutorial (http://code.google.com/apis/gdata/articles/java_client_lib.html),
I started yesterday to make a java class to get the names of my Google Docs.
Things work when I run my java project on a stand-alone basis.  When I
try to interface with R I run into troubles.  I've interfaced
Java code before, but I cannot find this problem.  A fresh set of
eyes may help.

On the R side, I create a package, I put all the required Google
jars and my RInterface.jar file in the inst/java directory.  I
have a .jpackage(pkgname) call in my .onLoad function.

When I call
   ref <- .jnew("dev/RInterface", username, password)
I get
Error in .jnew("dev/RInterface", username, password) :
   Failed to create object of class `dev/RInterface'
In addition: Warning message:
In .jnew("dev/RInterface", username, password) :
   NewObject("dev/RInterface","(Ljava/lang/String;Ljava/lang/String;)V",...) 
failed

So R sees the signature, but cannot create the RInterface object.
Things work If I don't create a DocsService object in the RInterface.

Sorry for the long email.  If you get me over this hump, I'll
pursue the project to have something workable soon.

Thanks,
  Adrian

I've attached my RInterface.java code.  Below is a simple main class.

import dev.RInterface;

public class testRInterface {

   public static void main(String[] args){
     RInterface R = new RInterface("USERNAME at gmail.com",
       "YOURPASSWORDHERE");

     String aux = R.getDocumentNames();
     System.out.println(aux);

   }
}

PS.  The google tutorial doesn't mention that you need to
register the jsr305.jar and google-collect-1.0.-rc1.jar to your
project.  These jars are in the gdata/java/deps folder.

> Hi,
>
> I have a strange problem when using JRI
>
> For example, I call this function written in test.R file
>
> test<- function()
> {
>      x<-3;
>      #x <- length(1:5);
>      return(x)
> }
>
> I interpret th result using the asInt() function, but I receive 0 not 3
>
> when I uncomment the 2nd line I do receive 5!!!!
>
> Many thanks for any help
> --
> Bilel


This is because 3 is parsed as a numeric in the expression "x <- 3". A 
few things you can do about it :

- explicitly use an integer with the "L" notation:

x <- 3L

- convert to integer :

as.integer( x )


The asInt method of the Rengine class seems confused:

BeanShell> r.getRni().eval( "test()" )
[REAL* (3.0)]
BeanShell> r.getRni().eval( "test()" ).asInt()
0

What you really should do is move on to the REngine API, which gets it 
well:

BeanShell> r.parseAndEval( "test()" ).asInteger()
3

Romain

Bilel,

On Jul 31, 2009, at 12:59 PM, Bilel MASMOUDI wrote:

> In order to let a java program using R transportable,
> So, I removed the %R_HOME%/bin and the %JRI_HOME% from the windows  
> path
> and I wrote this code to modify the path dynamically :
>
>         String path = System.getProperty("java.class.path");
>         path += ";C:\\R\\R-2.9.0\\bin";
>         path += ";C:\\R\\R-2.9.0\\library\\rJava\\jri";
>         System.out.println(path);
>         System.setProperty("java.class.path", path);
>

This is all wrong - the *class* path is not relevant to locating R  
(and the above has no effect anyway since the setting is only honored  
at startup), it is the *library* path (and the system PATH variable -  
though only on Windows) that matters. What you need to do first is to  
set the PATH to include the "bin" directory of your R (unfortunately  
you cannot do that form Java without 3rd party hacks). Then you have  
to make sure that all Java-related settings are in place and add the  
path to JRI to the java.library.path when you are starting Java.  
Please have a look at the JGR launcher - with --debug you'll see all  
the settings in C:\JGRdebug.txt.

As Bernd pointed out there is an issue of a flexible class path as  
well (it's necessary for JGR so other Java packages can be loaded -  
whether your app needs is up to you), we solve that by bootstrapping  
using the rJava class loader that can modify the class path at will  
(again, see the JGR startup sequence).

Cheers,
Simon
